reading.body:
AI adoption in US churches is not tracked by any official census; it is measured by a patchwork of research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes.

The pattern is measurement by survey and platform rather than by census. Barna Group runs the closest thing to sector-wide survey data, Gloo reports deployment across thousands of US churches, and Hartford and Pew add congregational and public attitude data. Census BTOS includes religious and civic organisations in its service-sector series, but no better official measure exists yet.

This matters for AI because adoption in churches is real but diffuse, and every tradition is writing its own guidance. The data does not say how many congregations actually use AI, how much compute that use requires, or what it means for power demand. It also does not give a single adoption rate, because none exists.

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The most concrete number available for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which reports that 15.0% of firms in Other services (NAICS 81, which includes religious organizations) answered yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, against 13.7% in the prior period. The survey first asked the question in September 2023, and some figures are suppressed, marked S. That 15.0% covers a broad NAICS category rather than congregations alone, so it is best read as the closest official measure rather than a church-specific count.

On the deployment side, Gloo describes itself as the sector's tech platform, delivering values-aligned models, developer tools and benchmarks for faith-based organizations, with AI as a foundational capability across its platform. Its AI Studio gives developers production environment tools, trusted content and values-aligned models, with API-first support for inference, RAG and assistant workflows and dynamic selection of the appropriate model for every request. This site's curated points describe Gloo as used by thousands of US churches and as a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations. Barna Group, a Christian research organization, is described here as running the national studies, with State of the Church work that quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception and use among US congregations and ministry leaders. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research, which has a 45 year history of providing accurate research on churches and congregational life, is cited for congregational technology surveys, though the harvested page text shows no AI figures.

AI and Faith convenes the ethics work, describing itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organizations working under five strategic pillars, and noting that 85 percent of the world's population claims a religious affiliation. It argues that the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI, and it frames itself as a pluralist organization seeking to engage the moral and ethical issues around artificial intelligence. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, is cited for research on AI and human formation, including a white paper from All Tech is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics lab titled Two Views of the Same Transformation.

That white paper reported that mid-level professionals described checking AI output as a growing, unrecognized share of their work, with some calling it babysitting AI slop, that this glue work of a rollout is missing from performance reviews, and that women reported carrying more of it. Executives, meanwhile, described middle management as a layer to cut and then worried about distributed deskilling. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher who often meets with AI leaders and developers, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and AI being able to do work faster and cheaper.

Pew Research Center measures public and clergy attitudes through its religion and public life work, and this site cites it for periodically measuring how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces. The harvested page text, however, covers religious hostilities, demographics and social attitudes rather than AI use, so it offers no adoption or spending figure here.

Across the material, no source reports a return-on-investment number for AI in congregations, and none describes a regulatory posture specific to churches. What a reader deciding whether to deploy can take from it is narrower: the official measure is a broad service-sector figure of 15.0%, the practical tooling conversation is being led by a faith-specific platform in Gloo and tracked by Barna's congregational research, and the ethical and human-formation questions are being pressed hardest by AI and Faith and by Notre Dame, where the reported risk is not failed software but unrecognized labor, deskilling and a flippant posture toward displacement.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, brings together a multidisciplinary community to advance moral understanding and respond to pressing ethical issues, including work on artificial intelligence and technology ethics that engages stakeholders to develop practical models for ethical design and deployment. A white paper from All Tech is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics lab, titled Two Views of the Same Transformation, reported that mid-level professionals described checking AI output as a growing and unrecognised part of their jobs, with some calling it "babysitting AI slop." That paper also found the glue work of a rollout is absent from performance reviews and that women reported carrying more of it, while executives described middle management as a layer to cut and then worried about distributed deskilling. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher at the University of Notre Dame who often meets AI leaders and developers, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper, and that some are trying to transcend work to spend their time on family and hobbies such as gardening and crafts.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group describes itself as a Christian research organization that supplies data and insights on trends affecting faith, culture and ministry. Its report, The State of Pastors, Volume 2, takes an in-depth look at how pastors are navigating post-pandemic life and ministry, focused on self-leadership, church leadership and cultural leadership, and a free webcast replay explores six trends shaping the future of pastoral leadership. A podcast hosted by pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas and Sharon Hodde Miller has them discussing church leadership challenges with guests, covering the health of the pastor and the state of the church. Barna also says young adults are motivated to attend church for a range of personal reasons ,  a search for identity, well-being and growth ,  and that one motivation stands out from all the rest.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organisations working toward a future in which AI serves humankind under five strategic pillars. The organisation argues that these issues are deeply moral at root, and ,  for the 85 percent of the world's population it says claims a religious affiliation ,  deeply spiritual too, with the world's religions offering ancient wisdom to guide AI's development and use. It says it encourages, connects and equips tech creators, academic researchers, ethicists and theologians to engage with the moral and ethical questions around AI and related technologies, aiming to shape the discussion in thoughtful, life-affirming ways. A statement quoted on the page frames the goal as injecting "humility and historicity" into an industry that has often rejected both, and as a humanistic effort to bring faith-based, literary, classical and oral traditions to bear on what it calls possibly the most important technological transformation of our time.
